sentences.text: A 2023 report revealed a juvenile Gorgosaurus fossil containing the intact remains of two juvenile Citipes in its stomach. The presence of only hindlimb and tail vertebrae suggests these young predators preferentially consumed the muscular hindlimbs of their prey.

More than twenty complete skeletons have been discovered, making it one of the best-represented tyrannosaurids in the fossil record. The longest known skull measures 99 centimeters, which is slightly smaller than that of Daspletosaurus.

The species Gorgosaurus libratus was first described by Lawrence Lambe in 1914. The genus Gorgosaurus was named by Lambe in 1914. The holotype specimen NMC 2120 was discovered in 1913 by Charles M. Sternberg.
Charles Whitney Gilmore named a small tyrannosaurid skull from Montana Gorgosaurus lancensis in 1946.

As an apex predator, Gorgosaurus preyed on abundant ceratopsids and hadrosaurs. In 1970, Dale Russell hypothesized that Gorgosaurus hunted fleet-footed hadrosaurs while Daspletosaurus hunted ceratopsians and ankylosaurians.
Evidence from Montana suggests Daspletosaurus also ate hadrosaurs, challenging the idea that it only hunted armored dinosaurs.
Researchers estimate that Gorgosaurus underwent a dietary shift when its lower jaw reached a length of 58 cm.

The holotype of Gorgosaurus libratus shows healed fractures on the 13th and 14th gastralia, the left fibula, and the third right dorsal rib. Another specimen bears a 10 cm longitudinal fracture in the middle of its right fibula.
Gorgosaurus spent up to half of its life in a juvenile phase before reaching near-maximum size in just a few years.
A Saurornitholestes jawbone found in the Dinosaur Park Formation bears tooth marks from a bite by a young tyrannosaur, possibly Gorgosaurus.
The main debate in Gorgosaurus paleobiology concerns whether it was a scavenger or a hunter, based on anatomical comparisons with coexisting tyrannosaurid species and ecological niche parameters.
Gorgosaurus is classified in the family Tyrannosauridae. It belongs to the parent group Albertosaurinae.

Gorgosaurus and Albertosaurus are extremely similar, with distinctions found mainly in subtle differences in their teeth and skull bones. Gorgosaurus is sometimes considered a junior synonym of Albertosaurus because Albertosaurus was named first. It is debated whether Gorgosaurus and Albertosaurus should be maintained as separate genera or combined into one. Some experts consider G. libratus to be a species of the genus Albertosaurus due to the extreme similarity between the two genera.
Some experts debate whether Gorgosaurus libratus is a distinct species or merely a synonym of the genus Albertosaurus.

Gorgosaurus lived in western North America during the Late Cretaceous Period (Campanian) between approximately 76.5 and 73 million years ago. Gorgosaurus lived in North America between 76.5 and 75.1 million years ago during the late Cretaceous period.

Gorgosaurus libratus fossils from the Dinosaur Park Formation date to between 76.6 and 75.1 million years ago during the middle Campanian stage. Fossils were found in the Dinosaur Park Formation of Alberta, Canada.
Gorgosaurus inhabited a lush floodplain environment located along the edge of an inland sea.
